literature.headline_zh: 马尔堡病毒持续性与诊断能力新进展。
literature.lead_zh: 近期两项研究揭示了马尔堡病毒在康复者体液中的潜在长期存在以及非洲实验室对该病毒的快速检测能力。
key_findings_zh: 卢旺达纵向研究将在康复后24个月内系统采集血、尿、精液等样本,评估马尔堡病毒的体液持续性及免疫保护[10.1136/bmjopen-2026-122687]。
几内亚分散实验室在2021年成功检测到马尔堡病毒病例,证明本地实验室可实现新兴病毒的快速识别[10.1038/s44298-026-00239-9]。
该实验室项目共检测4683例疑似VHF样本,发现47例阳性(1%),其中包括拉沙热30例,死亡率高达67.9%[10.1038/s44298-026-00239-9]。
两项工作均强调加强持续监测和本地实验室能力是降低病毒传播风险、提升公共卫生应对的关键[10.1136/bmjopen-2026-122687][10.1038/s44298-026-00239-9]。
literature.trend_or_risk_zh: 马尔堡病毒可能在康复者体液中长期存留,若缺乏监测可能导致二次传播;本地实验室能力提升有助于早期发现并遏制暴发。
literature.caveats_zh: 卢旺达研究仍在进行中,结果尚未公布;几内亚检测受样本来源偏倚影响,需扩大覆盖范围。
literature.headline_en: New Insights into Marburg Virus Persistence and Diagnostic Capacity.
literature.lead_en: Recent studies from Rwanda and Guinea reveal potential long‐term Marburg virus shedding in survivors and demonstrate local labs’ ability to rapidly detect the pathogen.
key_findings_en: A prospective cohort in Rwanda will follow survivors for 24 months, serially sampling blood, urine, semen and other fluids to characterize Marburg virus persistence and protective immunity [10.1136/bmjopen-2026-122687]

Guinea’s decentralized laboratory network identified a Marburg virus case during the 2021 outbreak, showing that in‐country labs can detect emerging hemorrhagic fevers promptly [10.1038/s44298-026-00239-9]

Across 4,683 suspected VHF specimens, 47 (1%) were positive, including 30 laboratory‐confirmed Lassa fever cases with a 67.9 % case‐fatality rate, underscoring the high burden of VHF in the region [10.1038/s44298-026-00239-9]

Both initiatives highlight that sustained surveillance and strengthened local diagnostic capacity are essential to mitigate transmission risk and improve outbreak response [10.1136/bmjopen-2026-122687][10.1038/s44298-026-00239-9]
literature.trend_or_risk_en: Marburg virus may persist in survivor fluids, posing a secondary transmission risk without systematic monitoring; enhanced local laboratory capacity reduces detection delays and outbreak spread.
literature.caveats_en: The Rwandan cohort is protocol‐only, with outcomes pending; Guinea’s data may reflect sampling bias and limited geographic coverage.
literature.brief_en: These findings collectively emphasize the need for long‐term monitoring of Marburg virus in survivors and for continued investment in decentralized laboratory networks in Africa to ensure rapid identification of hemorrhagic fever outbreaks.

papers.title: Marburg virus persistence and clinical complications among recovered persons in Rwanda: a longitudinal study protocol.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Marburg virus (MARV) causes a potentially highly lethal haemorrhagic fever disease that threatens global health security, and knowledge of viral persistence, long-term clinical outcomes among recovered persons and protective immunity remain limited. Existing protocols and technical guidelines provide a framework for safe sample collection, clinical monitoring and outbreak response, yet systematic approaches to investigate these aspects in African settings are scarce. This protocol describes the Partnership Research on MARV (PREMAV) following the 2024 outbreak in Rwanda. PREMAV is a longitudinal study that was initiated to investigate the persistence of MARV in body fluids of recovered persons, characterises associated clinical complications, identifies factors associated with viral persistence, classifies the protective immune response and discovers genomic variants during viral persistence. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a protocol for a prospective cohort study that enrolled individuals who survived Marburg virus disease (MVD), individuals with natural antibodies for MARV, close contacts and low risk controls in Rwanda. Participants will undergo serial sampling of blood, urine, semen and other relevant specimens over 24 months post-recovery. This will be combined with continuous clinical assessments, and laboratory analyses will include molecular detection, serological profiling, immunological assays and genomic viral characterisation. Statistical analysis will integrate the various datasets to determine associations. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study will adhere to the Declaration of Helsinki and obtain approval from the Rwanda National Ethics Committee. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants with additional safeguards for vulnerable groups. Confidentiality will be ensured through de-identification and secure data storage. All biological samples will be handled in compliance with national and international biosafety standards. Psychosocial support will be provided to address stigma and mental health needs among survivors. The study will generate critical evidence on MARV persistence, clinical sequelae and risk factors, informing survivor care guidelines, transmission mitigation strategies and future outbreak preparedness. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences and policy briefs targeting national and global stakeholders. De-identified data and genomic sequences will be curated and shared through secure platforms and public repositories in line with ethical and regulatory requirements.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决对马尔堡病毒(MARV)持续存在、康复者长期临床结局以及保护性免疫方面的知识不足,鉴于其对全球卫生安全的潜在威胁以及在非洲环境中系统性研究方法的匮乏。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 为调查MARV在康复者体液中的持续存在、描述相关临床并发症、识别与病毒持续存在相关的因素、分类保护性免疫应答,并在病毒持续存在期间发现基因组变异,制定了纵向研究方案。该方案在卢旺达实施。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究将纳入幸存马尔堡病毒病(MVD)的个体、具有天然抗MARV抗体的个体、密切接触者和低风险对照组。参与者将在康复后24个月内进行血、尿、精液及其他相关样本的连续采集,并结合持续的临床评估,实验室分析将包括分子检测、血清学分析、免疫学检测和病毒基因组特征分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 本研究旨在产生关于MARV持续存在、临床后遗症和风险因素的关键证据,并通过同行评审的出版物、会议和针对国家及全球利益相关者的政策简报进行传播。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果将为幸存者护理指南、传播缓解策略以及未来暴发的准备提供信息,为了解MARV感染的持续存在和临床结局提供新的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 本研究将提供关键证据,以改善幸存者护理、缓解传播风险并提高未来暴发的应对能力,对监测、诊断和治疗的马尔堡病毒病具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性包括由于纳入幸存者和密切接触者而可能存在的选择偏倚,以及其结果可能仅适用于卢旺达的特定背景。由于前瞻性队列研究设计和全面的样本采集与分析方案,证据强度为中等。

papers.title_zh: 马尔堡病毒在卢旺达康复者中的持续存在及临床并发症:一项纵向研究方案。
papers.source_body_en: INTRODUCTION: Marburg virus (MARV) causes a potentially highly lethal haemorrhagic fever disease that threatens global health security, and knowledge of viral persistence, long-term clinical outcomes among recovered persons and protective immunity remain limited. Existing protocols and technical guidelines provide a framework for safe sample collection, clinical monitoring and outbreak response, yet systematic approaches to investigate these aspects in African settings are scarce. This protocol describes the Partnership Research on MARV (PREMAV) following the 2024 outbreak in Rwanda. PREMAV is a longitudinal study that was initiated to investigate the persistence of MARV in body fluids of recovered persons, characterises associated clinical complications, identifies factors associated with viral persistence, classifies the protective immune response and discovers genomic variants during viral persistence. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a protocol for a prospective cohort study that enrolled individuals who survived Marburg virus disease (MVD), individuals with natural antibodies for MARV, close contacts and low risk controls in Rwanda. Participants will undergo serial sampling of blood, urine, semen and other relevant specimens over 24 months post-recovery. This will be combined with continuous clinical assessments, and laboratory analyses will include molecular detection, serological profiling, immunological assays and genomic viral characterisation. Statistical analysis will integrate the various datasets to determine associations. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study will adhere to the Declaration of Helsinki and obtain approval from the Rwanda National Ethics Committee. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants with additional safeguards for vulnerable groups. Confidentiality will be ensured through de-identification and secure data storage. All biological samples will be handled in compliance with national and international biosafety standards. Psychosocial support will be provided to address stigma and mental health needs among survivors. The study will generate critical evidence on MARV persistence, clinical sequelae and risk factors, informing survivor care guidelines, transmission mitigation strategies and future outbreak preparedness. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences and policy briefs targeting national and global stakeholders. De-identified data and genomic sequences will be curated and shared through secure platforms and public repositories in line with ethical and regulatory requirements.
papers.abstract_zh: INTRODUCTION: 马尔堡病毒 (MARV) 引起一种潜在高度致命的出血热疾病,威胁全球卫生安全,目前对病毒持续存在、康复者长期临床结局以及保护性免疫方面的知识仍有限。现有的协议和技术指南为安全样本采集、临床监测和暴发反应提供了框架,但在非洲环境中的系统性研究方法却很少。本方案描述了在卢旺达2024年暴发后开展的马尔堡病毒(MARV)合作研究(PREMAV)。PREMAV是一项纵向研究,旨在调查康复者体液中MARV的持续存在,描述相关临床并发症,识别与病毒持续存在相关的因素,分类保护性免疫应答,并在病毒持续存在期间发现基因组变异。METHODS AND ANALYSIS: 本方案为一项前瞻性队列研究研究的协议,纳入了在卢旺达幸存马尔堡病毒病(MVD)的个体、具有天然抗MARV抗体的个体、密切接触者和低风险对照组。参与者将在康复后24个月内进行血、尿、精液及其他相关样本的连续采集,并结合持续的临床评估,实验室分析将包括分子检测、血清学分析、免疫学检测和病毒基因组特征分析。统计分析将整合各种数据集以确定相关性。ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: 本研究将遵循赫尔辛基宣言,并获得卢旺达国家伦理委员会的批准。所有参与者将获得书面知情同意,对弱势群体将采取额外的保护措施。通过去标识化和安全的数据存储确保保密性。所有生物样本将按照国家和国际生物安全标准进行处理。将提供心理社会支持,以应对幸存者的污名和心理健康需求。本研究将产生关于MARV持续存在、临床后遗症和风险因素的关键证据,为幸存者护理指南、传播缓解策略以及未来暴发的准备提供信息。研究结果将通过同行评审的出版物、会议和针对国家及全球利益相关者的政策简报进行传播。去标识化的数据和基因组序列将通过安全平台和公共数据库进行整理和共享,符合伦理和监管要求。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决对马尔堡病毒(MARV)持续存在、康复者长期临床结局以及保护性免疫方面的知识不足,鉴于其对全球卫生安全的潜在威胁以及在非洲环境中系统性研究方法的匮乏。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 为调查MARV在康复者体液中的持续存在、描述相关临床并发症、识别与病毒持续存在相关的因素、分类保护性免疫应答,并在病毒持续存在期间发现基因组变异,制定了纵向研究方案。该方案在卢旺达实施。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究将纳入幸存马尔堡病毒病(MVD)的个体、具有天然抗MARV抗体的个体、密切接触者和低风险对照组。参与者将在康复后24个月内进行血、尿、精液及其他相关样本的连续采集,并结合持续的临床评估,实验室分析将包括分子检测、血清学分析、免疫学检测和病毒基因组特征分析。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果将为幸存者护理指南、传播缓解策略以及未来暴发的准备提供信息,为了解MARV感染的持续存在和临床结局提供新的见解。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 本研究将提供关键证据,以改善幸存者护理、缓解传播风险并提高未来暴发的应对能力,对监测、诊断和治疗的马尔堡病毒病具有重要意义。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性包括由于纳入幸存者和密切接触者而可能存在的选择偏倚,以及其结果可能仅适用于卢旺达的特定背景。由于前瞻性队列研究设计和全面的样本采集与分析方案,证据强度为中等。

papers.title: Strengthening diagnostic capacity for viral hemorrhagic fevers in Forest Guinea: advances in Lassa fever case detection
papers.abstract: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) remain a major public health threat in resource-limited settings. The 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic exposed critical gaps in laboratory preparedness and diagnostic capacity in most-at-risk countries, including Guinea. In order to implement sustainable in-country laboratory capacity for early detection and rapid response to VHF outbreaks, a decentralized diagnostics laboratory strengthening program started in the forested region of Guinea in Guéckédou (2017) and N'Zérékoré (2021). Between 2017 and 2024, a total of 4683 samples from suspected VHF cases were tested across the two laboratories. Of those, 47 (1%) were identified as positive for VHFs by molecular testing, including the 2021 Ebola virus disease resurgence and Marburg virus disease emergence samples, for which the laboratories supported rapid outbreak detection and response. Notably, 30 Lassa fever cases were laboratory-confirmed with a case fatality rate of 67.9%. Of those, 50.0% and 27.6% of the cases originating from the Guéckédou and N'Zérékoré prefecture, respectively. Prior to this program, Lassa fever detection in Guinea remained anecdotic. One case of yellow fever and one of dengue were also identified by molecular assays. The establishment of locally embedded laboratory capacity enhanced VHFs preparedness, surveillance, and response in Guinea, supporting Lassa fever epidemiology and health-system resilience.

analysis_zh.main_results: 在4683份样本中,47例(1%)被确认为VHF阳性,其中包括30例拉沙热病例,病死率为67.9%。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究证实了本地嵌入的实验室能力在增强几内亚对VHF的准备、监测和响应能力中的重要性,支持了拉沙热流行病学和卫生系统韧性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调了在资源匮乏地区持续投资实验室能力的必要性,以提高对VHF 暴发的早期检测和快速响应能力。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性包括可能存在抽样偏差以及需要更大的样本量以推广研究结果,其证据强度评估为中等。}}.{

Ebola Disease: Current Situation CDC is monitoring an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Learn more: Ebola Outbreak: Current Situation. For travelers returning to the United States from DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan, visit: Information for Travelers Returning from Ebola-Affected Areas. At a glance CDC established an office in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2002. CDC collaborates closely with the Government of DRC, the Ministry of Health (MOH), and various partners to build effective public health collaboration and partnerships to detect, prevent, and respond to global public health threats. CDC's work aims to protect the health of Americans and support public health around the world. Key accomplishments Pioneering electronic integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) using the DHIS2 platform in six provinces, allowing real-time surveillance reporting with integrated laboratory results, to improve the 7-1-7 model for outbreak responses in the DRC. Mentored 16 laboratories towards ISO 15189 accreditation, including two that became DRC’s first internationally accredited clinical laboratories in 2025. Established diagnostic capacities for HIV, monkeypox, and viral hemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Marburg Virus Disease and Ebola), and supported installation of a lab information system in 10 laboratories to streamline operations. Supported the training of 925 disease detectives through the Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), trained 120 MOH staff in emergency management, and educated over 3,800 healthcare providers in malaria diagnosis and treatment. Deployed staff and lab equipment to the 2025 Ebola outbreak (16th Ebola outbreak in DRC) in Bulape to support surveillance and laboratory testing. Supported the Ebola Treatment Unit laboratory to perform specimen testing for patient follow up. Provided technical support for surveillance and tetanus vaccination campaigns that led to the elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus in 2019. Contributed to the recent monkeypox and Ebola responses through laboratory testing, case investigations, infection prevention and control, risk communication, and community engagement. Global health security The Ministry of Health works with healthcare workers to monitor contacts of people diagnosed with Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak. SOURCE: Photo by Mary Claire Worrell/CDC DRC has a large population, spans a vast geographic area, and shares borders with nine other countries. CDC, MOH, and various partners collaborate to prevent, detect, respond to, and control infectious disease outbreaks within the country. CDC was the major partner who worked with the MOH to establish the National Public Health Institute (NPHI) in 2022, which coordinates essential public health functions such as preparedness and outbreak response, surveillance, laboratory systems, and workforce development. Laboratory strengthening CDC has successfully accredited two laboratories to ISO 15189 standards. Additionally, CDC helped develop a national laboratory strategic plan that directs the strengthening of laboratory systems in DRC. This includes donating essential equipment and enhancing laboratory diagnostics, network optimization, and quality management systems to meet the growing demand for early diagnosis of infectious diseases. CDC also supported the installation of a laboratory information system (LIS) in 10 laboratories to streamline their processes. Furthermore, CDC has provided training for laboratory staff and monitored testing quality through an external quality assurance program. Workforce development DRC’s FETP currently offers three levels of training: frontline, intermediate, and advanced. Participants enhance their skills in data collection and the translation of data into evidence-based actions. FETP graduates primarily include national and district public health staff, whose expertise has been vital in DRC’s responses to monkeypox, Ebola, COVID-19, and cholera. CDC has supported more than 900 FETP deployers throughout the country to participate in polio surveillance, monkeypox and Ebola outbreak responses, vaccination campaigns, and other immunization activities. Through FETP, CDC strengthens DRC’s workforce capacity to identify and contain outbreaks before they escalate globally. Ebola 2026 Ebola Outbreak: What CDC is Doing CDC is working with international partners on this evolving situation. CDC has taken proactive measures to prevent Ebola from entering the United States. news.source_body_en: The CDC is monitoring an Ebola disease outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). This information was published on September 15, 2026, and references the 2025 Ebola outbreak in Bulape, where CDC deployed staff and lab equipment to support surveillance and testing. The DRC has a large population and shares borders with nine other countries, making it a significant location for public health efforts. CDC collaborates with the DRC Ministry of Health and various partners to detect, prevent, and respond to infectious disease outbreaks. The risk to the American public and travelers remains low, and no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States due to this outbreak. CDC has supported the training of 925 disease detectives and 120 MOH staff, as well as the installation of a lab information system in 10 laboratories to improve outbreak response. The CDC also played a major role in establishing the National Public Health Institute (NPHI) in 2022, which coordinates essential public health functions. These efforts aim to strengthen the DRC's capacity to identify and contain outbreaks before they escalate globally.

news.content_title: A Scientist Bled to Death for Two Weeks. The Virus He Left Behind Is Sitting in His Lab.
news.content: 4 min read Key Points A Soviet scientist died agonizingly from Marburg virus after accidentally infecting himself during weaponization research at a Siberian biolab. The virus mutated into a deadlier strain inside the infected researcher's body, which Soviet bioweapons scientists then weaponized into powder for potential biological attacks. The weaponized Marburg variant remains stored at a Russian research facility today, raising ongoing concerns about accidental or intentional release decades after the Cold War. Many stories and secrets were lost in the ash heap of the Soviet Union’s collapse. But one fact is not in doubt: Dr. Nikolai Ustinov died painfully. “I can say it was a terrible death,” said Dr. Ken Alibek, formerly Dr. Kanatjan Alibekov, in a 1998 Frontline documentary . “He was dying for about two weeks. It was blood from everywhere, from nose, from eyes, mouth, ears.” Dr. Ustinov had become infected with a disease for which there was no cure. From the moment he contracted Marburg virus (MARV), a member of the Filoviridae family with symptoms similar to its cousin Ebola, his fate was sealed. But while Marburg infections typically come from an exchange of bodily fluids with an infected person, or contact with an Egyptian fruit bat, the manner in which Dr. Ustinov came to be infected is something stranger and far more sinister. Dr. Nikolai Ustinov worked at the State Research Center of Virology and Biotechnology, also known as VECTOR, conducting research at their maximum-security BSL-4 lab in Koltsovo, Siberia. Ustinov was researching the deadly Marburg virus, but not with the intention to find a cure; his work to better understand the disease was with an aim toward weaponizing it. There’s some disagreement as to just how Ustinov contracted Marburg himself. While it’s agreed that an accident occurred in the course of his daily research activity—purposefully infecting guinea pigs with the horrific bleeding disease via syringe—two stories have emerged for how it happened. The aforementioned Frontline report alludes to a second scientist being in the lab, whose syringe-wielding hand slipped and jabbed the finger of Ustinov, who was holding the next small, furry, soon-to-be viral victim. But Annie Jacobsen’s Biological War suggests that Ustinov made the error entirely himself, accidentally injecting his own finger instead of the guinea pig. Once Ustinov realized what had happened, Jacobsen recounts, he took action: “Dr. Ustinov quickly left the lab through one of Vector’s airlocks, took a chemical shower to decontaminate the biohazard suit he was wearing, and used an emergency telephone to call his boss. His supervisor instructed him to go to Vector’s biocontainment hospital, also equipped with submarine-like airlocks.” Ustinov’s wife Yevgenia could only see her husband through a window, and could only speak to him via a telephone, up to and including their final goodbye. She was spared, however, seeing the extent of what the deadly virus was doing to him; his colleagues, according to Frontline , “wrapped him in sheets to his chin during her visits.” But Ustinov understood that his colleagues did need to know the details of what the virus was doing to him. They were viral researchers, after all, and his infection offered a singular opportunity to advance their knowledge. “With clinical detachment,” the U.S. Naval War College recounts in an article on the event, “he documented his own decline in a journal with bloodspotted pages.” Following his death, a team of biohazard suit-adorned doctors went to work conducting an autopsy on Ustinov. They extracted his spleen and liver and removed his blood via syringe. What they discovered was that, while the virus was slowly killing Dr. Ustinov, it was also evolving inside him. “It had transformed,” Jacobsen writes, “into a far more virulent germ than the original strain of Marburg virus Dr. Ustinov had been working with when he accidentally stuck himself with that syringe.” Ustinov’s remains were placed in a “zinc-lined coffin,” and the new strain that had developed in his body was named “Variant U” in his honor.
